alternatives.note: His father's notebook uses the Florentine year, which began on March 25; by the Roman reckoning the year is 1475.
Roster year agrees with the preferred date.
Roster year agrees with the cited sources.

historical_timeline.summary: His father dies at about ninety.
Proposed onset of hand osteoarthritis, from portraits (retrospective).
Writes that his doctors think he has calculus; severe pain and sleeplessness.
Passes fragments of the stone after drinking a mineral water.
Has drunk a stone-breaking spring water for two months and must change his way of life.
Writes of the stone, side and back pain, and difficulty with stairs.
Writes that writing is very troublesome to his hand, eyes, and memory.
Reported ill and restless, out in the rain, with uncertain speech.
Dies in Rome, within a few weeks of his 89th birthday.

claims.statement: Michelangelo was born at Caprese on March 6, 1475, by the modern reckoning; his father's notebook records the birth as March 6, 1474, in the Florentine style, on a Monday morning before daybreak.
He died in Rome a little before five o'clock in the afternoon of February 18, 1564, within a few weeks of his 89th birthday, attended to the end by two physicians.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The contemporary letters describe a short final illness; its cause cannot be determined.

claims.statement: A friend's letter of February 14, 1564, reported finding him out on foot in the rain, saying he was ill and could not find rest anywhere, with uncertain speech; he spent his last four days partly in an armchair and partly in bed.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Symonds describes this as a kind of seizure; the nature of the illness is not determined.

claims.statement: In 1548 he wrote to his nephew that he had lately been in great difficulty from dysuria but was better.

In a letter to his nephew dated March 15, 1549, he wrote that he had been very ill with dysuria, groaning in pain night and day without sleep, that his doctors thought he was suffering from calculus, and that he had been advised to try the baths at Viterbo.
On March 23, 1549, he wrote that after drinking a water sent to him he passed a large quantity of thick white matter with portions of the shell of the stone, and was much better.
On April 5, 1549, he wrote that it was now quite certain that he had urinary calculus, not very advanced, and that it was gradually diminishing with the water he was drinking.

In a letter the editor dates to June 8, 1549, he wrote that for about two months he had drunk, morning and evening, a water from a spring about forty miles from Rome that breaks up the stone, that it had broken his and let him pass water with tolerable ease, and that he would have to use nothing else for drinking or cooking and alter his mode of life.

source_links.locator: Letter dated by the editor June 8, 1549

claims.statement: On June 16, 1557, he wrote to his nephew that he suffered from all the ailments of old age: the stone, so that he could not pass water, and pains in his side and back, so that he often could not go up or down stairs.
A postscript to a letter of 1559 (dated June 15; the editor notes the nephew altered it to July 15) reads: writing is very troublesome to my hand, my eyes and my memory; such is the effect of age.

Lazzeri and colleagues (2016), studying portraits, proposed that degenerative, non-inflammatory osteoarthritis affected the base of his left thumb, the thumb's metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints, and the index finger's metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints; earlier portraits show no deformity, and they place the onset around 1547 to 1553, with worsening in his last fifteen years.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A retrospective diagnosis from paintings; no skeletal or radiographic evidence exists.

claims.statement: The same authors report that letters to his nephew speak of gout, a period term for many arthritic conditions, and of a cruel pain in one foot; they judged gouty arthritis of the hands unlikely because the portraits show no inflammation or tophi.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The gout is a retrospective reading of period language; the original letters about gout were not located in the edition consulted.

claims.statement: Lazzeri and colleagues report that he was seen hammering up to six days before his death, and suggest that his continued, intense work helped him keep the use of his hands.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The suggestion about function is the authors' interpretation.

claims.statement: His father, Lodovico, was born on June 11, 1444, and died in 1533 or 1534; Michelangelo's poem on his death says he was ninety.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The cause of death is not recorded in the source.

claims.statement: He had two acute illnesses, the first in the summer of 1544 and the second toward the close of 1545, when news reached Florence that he was dying; he recovered from both.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The nature of the illnesses is not recorded in the cited source.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Manage hand osteoarthritis in an 85-year-old sculptor who still works with hammer and chisel, by the 2019 ACR/Arthritis Foundation guideline and the CMID osteoarthritis schedule: confirm the diagnosis clinically and exclude inflammatory, crystal, and iron-overload arthritis when the metacarpophalangeal joints are involved; put exercise, hand therapy, joint protection, and a thumb-base splint first; use topical rather than oral NSAIDs, stopping self-directed ibuprofen because of age, kidney function, and blood pressure; offer a thumb-base glucocorticoid injection; measure pain, function, and grip at each visit; keep him working; and keep well-controlled gout and a past stone history quiet while assessing falls.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Buonarroti returns four weeks after stopping over-the-counter ibuprofen 1200 mg a day and starting diclofenac gel four times daily, acetaminophen as needed, and a left thumb-base splint. He uses the gel faithfully and takes acetaminophen 1 g about twice a day. His hand pain is somewhat better, about 5 of 10, but gripping a chisel for more than an hour still brings on a deep ache at the base of the left thumb, and morning stiffness lasts about 15 minutes. He wears the splint for carving and at night. He has not yet started hand therapy because of a waiting list. He has had no gout flare, urinary symptoms, rash, or stomach upset. He saw the rheumatologist this morning and had the thumb-base injection.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Buonarroti is an 85-year-old sculptor with hand osteoarthritis, worst at the base of the left thumb, and gout in remission, who came in the same morning after cutting his left index finger. About two hours ago, while roughing out a block, the chisel slipped from his left hand and the edge cut the back of the index finger. He says his pinch grip gave way; he was working without his thumb splint because it was being cleaned. The bleeding stopped with ten minutes of pressure. He can bend and straighten the finger fully and has no numbness. The tools were clean steel; there was marble dust in the wound. He takes no blood thinners. His last tetanus booster was more than ten years ago. He took acetaminophen 1 g for the pain.

referral.question: Painful, stiff hands in an 85-year-old working sculptor, worst at the left thumb base, with metacarpophalangeal as well as interphalangeal involvement. Please confirm osteoarthritis, exclude inflammatory, crystal, and iron-overload arthritis, and advise on a thumb-base injection and on safe pain relief that lets him keep carving
referral.pertinent_history: Two years of worsening left thumb-base pain and stiffness, with knobby swelling of the left thumb and index finger; carving now limited to about two hours and writing to short notes. He had been taking ibuprofen 1200 mg a day for three months; today creatinine is 1.21 mg/dL (eGFR 59) and blood pressure 148/82, so ibuprofen was stopped and diclofenac gel, acetaminophen as needed, and a thumb-base splint started. Gout without tophi, in remission on allopurinol 200 mg, serum urate 5.4 mg/dL; urinary stones years ago, none since. Radiographs today: left first carpometacarpal osteoarthritis (Eaton stage III), narrowing and osteophytes at the left thumb and index metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints, right distal interphalangeal osteophytes, no erosions or chondrocalcinosis. CRP 2.1 mg/L, ESR 18 mm/h, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP negative, ferritin 110 ng/mL, transferrin saturation 28%. Pain 7 of 10; PROMIS upper extremity T-score 33; grip 14 kg left, 22 kg right
questions: Do you agree this is osteoarthritis, and is anything else, such as calcium pyrophosphate disease, hemochromatosis, gout, or an inflammatory arthritis, contributing given the metacarpophalangeal involvement?
Is a glucocorticoid injection of the left thumb base appropriate, and would you perform it?
What pain relief is safe at 85 with gout, a past stone history, and a creatinine rise on ibuprofen?
What splinting, hand therapy, and tool changes do you advise so he can keep carving?
Does his gout need any change in treatment because of the hand symptoms?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Buonarroti is seen at the request of Dr. Castellano for hand pain. He has carved stone all his working life and still works most mornings. Over about two years the base of his left thumb has become painful and stiff, with knobby swelling of the thumb and index finger and, more recently, the right index and middle fingertips. Morning stiffness lasts about 15 minutes. He has had no hot, swollen hand joints, no rash, psoriasis, or nail change, and no other joint symptoms apart from his past gout, which has been quiet on allopurinol. After four weeks off ibuprofen and on diclofenac gel and a splint, his pain is about 5 of 10
